name: Thai Basil
summary: A warm-season branching basil with a distinct anise-clove profile. Garden treats it as basil structurally, while keeping cultivar-level height and naming differences visible across sources.

metrics.label: Height reference
metrics.note: Home Grown vs. UMN variety context

germination.guidance: Thai basil is a warm-season basil. Johnny's Sweet Thai reference and Home Grown both support about 5–10 days to germination under warm seed-starting conditions.

thinning.short: Thin by vigor and canopy crowding, not field inches
thinning.guidance: Field sources use wide final spacing, but a compact pod should not copy that number literally. Keep the strongest stems and reduce only when seedlings compete strongly for the same light path or root volume.

pruning.short: Pinch above a healthy node to branch
pruning.guidance: Use basil's normal branching logic: once established, remove a growing tip just above a healthy leaf pair or node. Regular top harvests can keep the plant compact and productive.

harvest.short: Begin lightly after establishment; harvest tops regularly
harvest.guidance: Home Grown starts harvest after several sets of leaves and about 12–18 inches, while stronger basil guidance allows light harvest once plants are established. Garden should use structure and recovery capacity rather than age alone.

flowering.short: Flowering marks a shift away from peak leaf production
flowering.guidance: For leaf-focused use, harvest before heavy flowering and keep the plant actively branching. Visible buds should still be recorded as a real stage, not treated as an error.

hydroponics.short: Use basil hydro targets as a crop-level reference
hydroponics.guidance: OSU lists basil at about EC 1.0–1.6 mS/cm and pH 5.5–6.0. Johnny's also identifies Thai basil types as suitable for hydroponic/container production. Shared-reservoir targets still need to respect the other crops in the system.

problems.short: Watch stress-driven flowering, crowding and weak light response
problems.guidance: Water stress and high heat can accelerate flowering in basil, while dense indoor growth can reduce airflow. Garden should interpret these signs together with actual history and photos.

evidence.note: Hydroponic basil production guidance applies at the species/crop level; it does not establish this named variety’s dimensions or performance.

name: Italian Large Leaf Basil
summary: A large-leaf culinary basil that follows the same node-based branching logic as Genovese while retaining its own manufacturer variety profile.

metrics.label: Germination
metrics.note: Home Grown; consistent with basil grower reference

germination.guidance: Home Grown lists 5–10 days for Italian Large Leaf, matching Johnny's general basil window under warm seed-starting conditions.

thinning.short: Keep vigorous stems; manage crowding rather than copying field spacing
thinning.guidance: Home Grown uses 12–18 inch field spacing, but Garden should translate that into canopy and root competition in a pod instead of a literal indoor spacing rule.

pruning.short: Cut above a node to preserve branching points
pruning.guidance: Once the plant is established, harvest or pinch stems just above a healthy node. This preserves active side shoots and is consistent across Home Grown, Johnny's and USU basil guidance.

harvest.short: Start around 6–8 inches when the plant can recover
harvest.guidance: Home Grown specifically allows harvest around 6–8 inches and recommends individual leaves or stems above a node. Garden should favor repeated light stem harvests over stripping a young plant.

flowering.short: Keep leaf production ahead of flowering
flowering.guidance: Regular harvest before heavy flowering supports continued leaf production. Flower buds are a stage signal that should influence, not automatically dictate, the next cut.

hydroponics.guidance: OSU lists basil at about EC 1.0–1.6 mS/cm and pH 5.5–6.0. Use this as a crop-level reference, not as a command to override a shared reservoir's current recipe.

problems.short: Crowding, water stress and flowering reduce leaf quality
problems.guidance: Basil needs strong light, steady moisture and airflow. Garden should distinguish ordinary mature flowering from stress-driven decline by using history and visual evidence together.

evidence.note: Hydroponic basil production guidance applies at the species/crop level; it does not establish this named variety’s dimensions or performance.

name: Florence Fennel
summary: A cool-season bulbing fennel grown for its swollen leaf bases as well as fronds. Root disturbance, heat and uneven moisture matter more than pruning.

germination.short: Cool-season seed with 7–10 day Extension reference
germination.guidance: USU lists Florence fennel germination at about 7–10 days when soil is 50–75°F. Home Grown gives a compatible broader 7–14 day window.

thinning.short: A bulbing crop needs one strong final crown per position
thinning.guidance: Unlike chives or bunching onion, Florence fennel needs room for one swollen base. In a pod or container, keep the strongest final seedling and avoid copying outdoor inch spacing literally.

pruning.guidance: Do not prune Florence fennel like basil. Preserve the active crown and fronds; if a seed stalk forms early, treat that as bolting rather than a normal shaping opportunity.

harvest.short: Harvest the firm bulbous base before it overmatures
harvest.guidance: USU recommends harvesting Florence fennel when the bulbous base is firm and less than about 4 inches across. Fronds may be used earlier as garnish without sacrificing the central crown.

flowering.short: Heat, long days and root stress can trigger bolting
flowering.guidance: Florence fennel performs best in cooler conditions. Heat, long days, water stress or root disturbance can accelerate bolting and reduce bulb quality.

hydroponics.short: Physical root and bulb geometry need validation first
hydroponics.guidance: Garden does not assign a precise hydroponic EC/pH target yet. Before recommending compact hydro culture, validate that the basket and root zone can accommodate a swollen base and taproot without chronic stress.

problems.short: Bolting, splitting and undersized bulbs are the main quality risks
problems.guidance: Keep moisture consistent and avoid root damage. A plant producing mostly fronds without a useful base may reflect heat, stress, variety mismatch or insufficient physical room.

name: Lemongrass
summary: A warm tropical clumping grass. The Home Grown guide identifies only Cymbopogon spp., so Garden keeps the exact species unresolved instead of silently choosing East- or West-Indian lemongrass.

germination.guidance: Home Grown gives 7–21 days at about 70°F. Johnny's East Indian lemongrass reference gives 7–14 days and notes that light aids germination. Garden keeps the broader group-level range until the packet species is resolved.

thinning.guidance: Lemongrass can be grown as a clump. Remove only weak or strongly competing seedlings when the young cluster is overcrowded; do not force a universal one-stem rule.

pruning.short: No branching prune; manage older outer stalks
pruning.guidance: Lemongrass does not need node-based pruning. Maintenance is mainly harvest and removal of older or damaged outer material while preserving the active central clump.

harvest.short: Take mature outer stalks from an established clump
harvest.guidance: USU and Johnny's both support harvesting mature outer stalks after establishment. Home Grown uses a smaller stalk-diameter cue than USU, so Garden preserves the species/context difference instead of enforcing one universal diameter.

flowering.short: Flowering is uncommon in short-season culture
flowering.guidance: Johnny's notes East Indian lemongrass rarely flowers when grown as an annual. Garden should treat any flowering as a real stage but not as a routine indoor milestone.

hydroponics.short: Large clump architecture makes compact hydro a special case
hydroponics.guidance: No crop-specific hydroponic nutrient target is accepted yet. The plant can become large and root-dense, so Garden should validate physical fit and reservoir behavior before recommending it for a small countertop system.

problems.short: Cold, low light and cramped root volume are major constraints
problems.guidance: Lemongrass is frost sensitive and strongly favors warm, bright conditions. In Utah, USU treats it as a tender perennial commonly grown as an annual or overwintered in containers.

name: Spearmint
summary: A vigorous perennial mint suited to repeated leaf harvest and tea use. Pinching encourages branching, while long-term crowding and root spread are more important than a fixed seedling count.

germination.short: Surface-sown mint with a 7–14 day variety reference
germination.guidance: Home Grown lists 7–14 days for spearmint. Johnny's generic mint reference gives 10–14 days and confirms that mint seed needs light, so Garden treats the ranges as compatible rather than conflicting.

thinning.short: Manage the clump by vigor and root crowding
thinning.guidance: Mint naturally spreads and branches. In a pod, retain healthy stems while the canopy is open, then reduce or divide when root mass, airflow or light competition becomes limiting.

pruning.short: Pinch tops regularly for bushier growth
pruning.guidance: Johnny's recommends pinching top sets of leaves from the seedling stage onward. Home Grown also recommends taking leaves just above a node, which fits the same branching logic.

harvest.guidance: Harvest individual leaves and tender stems once the plant is established. For larger cuts, take stems above healthy nodes and leave enough active growth for recovery.

flowering.short: Whole-plant harvest peaks just before flowering
flowering.guidance: Johnny's recommends whole-plant harvest just before flowering, while individual leaves can be taken earlier. Garden should keep flowering as a stage cue rather than a failure condition.

hydroponics.guidance: Garden does not assign a precise spearmint EC/pH range yet. The bigger practical constraint in a small system may be vigorous root and canopy spread rather than nutrient demand alone.

problems.short: Vigorous spread and crowding are the main structural risks
problems.guidance: USU and Johnny's both describe mint as aggressive or invasive in soil. In a hydroponic pod, translate that into periodic root/canopy crowding checks rather than an outdoor containment warning.
